The test showed a significant positive DRB effect in green-background trials (M = 18 ms, SD = 38 ms), t(62) = 3.76, p < .001, d = 0.47, 95% CI [8 ms, 27 ms]. This confirmed strong distractor–response binding when the background context was a red hue. As with the green condition, this post hoc test decomposed the three-way interaction from the RT ANOVA.

The DRB effects for both RTs and error rates were calculated with this formula: (RR-DC-trials − RR-DR-trials) − (RC-DC-trials − RC-DR-trials), with RR/RC standing for response repetition/response change and DR/DC for distractor (color) repetition/change. This corresponds to the benefit of distractor color repetition in response repetition trials minus the cost of distractor color repetition in response change trials.
...
In the green background condition, significant DRB effects could be observed: M = 18 ms, SD = 38 ms, two-tailed t(62) = 3.76, p < .001, d = 0.47, 95% confidence interval (CI) [8 ms, 27 ms]. In the red background condition, the observed DRB effects were stronger: M = 35 ms, SD = 34 ms, two-tailed t(62) = 8.26, p < .001, d = 1.04, 95% CI [27 ms, 44 ms].
...
The DRB effect for response and distractor stimuli was then used as a dependent variable to compare red and green background conditions.

The DRB effects for both RTs and error rates were calculated with this formula: (RR-DC-trials − RR-DR-trials) − (RC-DC-trials − RC-DR-trials), with RR/RC standing for response repetition/response change and DR/DC for distractor (color) repetition/change. This corresponds to the benefit of distractor color repetition in response repetition trials minus the cost of distractor color repetition in response change trials. 2 DRB effects were compared with post hoc t tests.

From all participants, trials with missing responses (for either prime or probe) were excluded from all further analyses (1.7% of trials), as well as another 4.3% of trials with wrong responses in the prime. 4.1% of probe errors (with correct responses in the prime) were used for error rate analyses. For RT analyses, another 3.2% of trials with probe RT below 200 ms and more than 1.5 interquartile ranges above the third quartile of each subject’s RT distribution were excluded (cf. Tukey, 1977). In total, 86.7% of all trials remained for RT analyses. Note that participants who were heavy outliers were excluded after the data filtering process.
